title: A nephew's warning (Acts 23)
hook: Paul's sister's son overhears an ambush plot and tells the commander
tomorrow: a governor hears about self-control and says: not now…

segments.voice: Paul tells his story on the castle stairs, and at its center is a question: what shall I do, Lord? Now he's held in that fortress, and the danger comes looking for him.
screen: `WHAT SHALL I DO, LORD?` → `HELD IN THE FORTRESS.`

segments.voice: Somebody's little brother sees a group chat he wasn't meant to see, and something in it is about a person you love. Does he say anything? In Jerusalem, a band of men swear an oath not to eat or drink until they've killed Paul; Acts says there were more than forty of them. And who overhears? Acts never gives his name or his age. He's simply "Paul's sister's son."
screen: `A CHAT HE WASN'T MEANT TO SEE.` → `AN OATH AND AN AMBUSH.` → `PAUL'S SISTER'S SON.`

segments.voice: Today's question: where does courage come from when you're being hunted? Acts gives two answers. The first comes the night before, in the fortress: "the Lord stood by him, and said, Be of good cheer, Paul." Today's line, take heart, is that phrase in plainer words. The second answer is a person. "And when Paul's sister's son heard of their lying in wait, he went and entered into the castle, and told Paul." Paul sends him to the commander, who "took him by the hand, and went with him aside privately, and asked him, What is that thou hast to tell me?" A powerful man, taking a young one by the hand. That same night Paul rides out of Jerusalem under heavy guard. Now a neighbor. Muslims remember a night of hiding too. The Qur'an recalls the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in a cave with one companion while men searched for them, and his words to his frightened friend, in Pickthall's translation: "Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us." Muslim tradition names the friend Abu Bakr, and the journey the Hijra. Here's the one to tell a friend tonight: in both stories, courage arrives in the dark as words, God is with you, before anyone is safe. The honest difference: in Acts, Christians hear the risen Lord himself standing by Paul and speaking. In the Qur'an, the Prophet speaks the comfort to his friend, and the verse says God sent down his peace.
screen: `WHERE DOES COURAGE COME FROM?` · `BE OF GOOD CHEER, PAUL.` · `A NEPHEW WALKS IN TO TELL.` · `A NEIGHBOR: GRIEVE NOT.` · then, large: `TAKE HEART, PAUL.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone who might need courage this week, or a warning that only you could pass on. Hold them there, and let two words rest on them: take heart. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.
A nephew's warning. A young man with no name who overheard an ambush plot and walked into the fortress to tell.
Hold on to this: take heart, Paul, words spoken in the dark before any rescue came. Go well.

fork.setup: a coworker mentions, half-joking, that a few people plan to blame the new hire for a mistake they made. the manager doesn't know. what fits Acts 23?
options: quietly tell the manager, who can actually act on it.
warn everyone in the break room so it can't happen.
stay out of it; it isn't your business to repeat.

chat.says: nia's brother heard kids plan to wreck her sculpture at the art show. he begged me not to tell.
options: Pass it to someone who can act, like the nephew did. Tell Nia and the art teacher, quietly.
Keep the promise. The nephew in Acts kept the plot to himself so no one got hurt.
Post a warning for everyone. The nephew told the whole city so the plotters backed off.
chat.meaning: Paul's nephew took what he overheard to Paul, then to the commander, privately. A warning goes to whoever can act on it.

Pickthall.meaning: an English translator of the Qur'an, published in 1930

Abu Bakr.meaning: the Prophet's companion in the cave, as Muslim tradition names him

Hijra.meaning: the Prophet Muhammad's journey from Mecca to Medina

sources.ref: Qur'an 9:40 (God sent down his peace of reassurance); the companion named Abu Bakr and the journey called the Hijra in Muslim tradition (e.g. Sahih al-Bukhari 3653)

notes: Acts 23:12 says 'certain of the Jews banded together'; the lesson says 'a band of men' and 'more than forty' (23:13) so a group of plotters isn't made to stand for a people. Confirm.
The index carry 'take heart, paul' renders the KJV 'Be of good cheer, Paul' (Acts 23:11); the teach says so. Some Greek texts of 23:11 lack the name Paul; left out under the claims rule.
'Under heavy guard' summarizes Acts 23:23 (soldiers, horsemen and spearmen); the numbers are left out of the voice for length.

UNITY THREAD (wisdom day): the neighbor is Islam. Qur'an 9:40 quoted from Pickthall 1930 ('Grieve not. Lo! Allah is with us.'), the same wording used on the Islam path (days 0697, 0766, 1396); confirm exact wording. 'God sent down his peace' paraphrases the rest of 9:40 (Pickthall: 'Allah caused His peace of reassurance to descend upon him'). The companion's name (Abu Bakr) and the Hijra are given as Muslim tradition; the hadith reference (Sahih al-Bukhari 3653) should be checked by a Muslim scholar.

The shared point (courage arrives in the dark as words, God is with you, before anyone is safe) and the honest difference (in Acts, Christians hear the risen Lord standing by Paul; in the Qur'an, the Prophet comforts his friend and the verse says God sent down his peace) are given without ranking. Confirm both are fair to each tradition, and that the Prophet is named with 'peace be upon him' the first time.
